topics.title: The Iran war reaches the Strait of Hormuz
topics.hook: In May 2026 the war that began with the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader in February spread into the Strait of Hormuz, and the world found out again how one narrow waterway can move the price of everything.
topics.story:
The war started on 28 February 2026. Israel and the United States launched simultaneous operations, code-named Roaring Lion and Epic Fury, that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and several senior commanders in a single night. The Israeli Air Force flew its largest combat sortie ever, hitting roughly 500 targets with over 1,200 bombs in 24 hours, and a cyberattack knocked out Iran's internet for more than 60 hours. Iran had been through a shorter round with Israel already, the Twelve-Day War of June 2025, which in hindsight looks like a rehearsal.

What followed was not a quick war. Iran struck back at Israel, the Gulf states and US bases. Hezbollah was drawn in from Lebanon. A two-week ceasefire opened on 8 April and fell apart within days; a round of talks in Islamabad on 12 and 13 April, with Pakistan's foreign minister Ishaq Dar shuttling between Washington and Tehran, produced nothing durable.

May is when the war reached the world's most important oil chokepoint. On 4 May, the US Navy launched Operation Project Freedom, escorting tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, the 33-kilometre-wide passage between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil moves. Iran's regular navy and its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy treated the escorts as provocation. On 7 May, Iran fired on three US destroyers, USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta and USS Mason; US Central Command answered with what it called self-defence strikes on Iranian military sites, and explosions were reported at the ports of Bandar Abbas and Qeshm. Washington insisted this was not a restart of full-scale war, a distinction that meant very little to shipping insurers, who priced Gulf transits as a war-risk zone through the month.

The casualty count by June, when a ceasefire finally held, ran into the thousands: Iran put its own dead at roughly 3,500 with over 26,000 injured, the US lost 19 soldiers and a contractor, and Israel recorded 38 soldiers and 31 civilians killed. Hezbollah alone reported over a thousand fighters dead.

India's stake in all this was never abstract. India imports more than four-fifths of its crude oil, and a large share of it moves through the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz on its way from Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the UAE. Every reported skirmish near Hormuz through May pushed Brent crude higher, and Indian refiners and the finance ministry watched the Strait the way they watch the monsoon: something they cannot control and have to plan the year's budget around anyway. Dubai airport reported a 66 percent drop in March passenger traffic because of the war, a preview of how disruption in one country's airspace cascades through a region India depends on for both energy and expatriate remittances.

By the end of May there was no peace deal, only a war that had not, for the moment, become a full naval blockade. The settlement that eventually stopped it, the Islamabad Memorandum, was still six weeks away.

topics.title: The Supreme Court upholds the Bihar electoral roll purge
topics.hook: On 27 May 2026 the Supreme Court closed the book on the Bihar Special Intensive Revision, ruling that striking 47 lakh names off the rolls before an election was lawful, proportionate and within the Election Commission's power.
topics.story:
The dispute went back to June 2025, when the Election Commission of India ordered a Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, of Bihar's electoral rolls ahead of that year's assembly election. The exercise started with 7.89 crore voters on the rolls. Every voter had to file fresh documents proving citizenship and residence; anyone who did not was struck off. By the time the final roll was published on 30 September 2025, the number had fallen to 7.42 crore, a drop of roughly 47 lakh names in three months.

The Association for Democratic Reforms and other petitioners went to the Supreme Court, arguing that the SIR was really a backdoor citizenship test dressed up as an administrative exercise, that it disproportionately hit the poor, migrant workers and minorities who struggle to produce paperwork on short notice, and that it was too rushed and too close to an election to be fair. The Election Commission's answer was that Article 324 of the Constitution gives it superintendence over elections precisely so it can keep the rolls clean, and that Section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 lets it revise rolls as it sees fit.

A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, sitting with Justice Joymalya Bagchi, took up the case through 2025 and into 2026, at one point directing the Commission to hand over details of the 3.66 lakh voters excluded from the final roll so their exclusions could be checked. The final judgment came on 27 May 2026, well after the Bihar election itself had already been held and its results declared on 14 November 2025 under the revised rolls.

The Court upheld the SIR as constitutional, procedurally sound and proportionate. It read Article 324 broadly, holding that an intensive revision serves the same purpose the Constitution assigns the Commission: an accurate roll is the precondition for a free and fair election, not an obstacle to one. On the citizenship question, the bench drew a careful line. The Commission can ask about citizenship while compiling rolls, because a non-citizen has no right to vote, but it cannot make a final, binding determination of anyone's citizenship status; that remains the job of the machinery set up under the Citizenship Act, 1955.

For an aspirant this case sits at the intersection of three things CLAT tests constantly: the Election Commission's constitutional status, the limits of executive and quasi-judicial power, and the recurring argument in Indian law over how much process is due before the state can take away a right. The result also carries forward: the same SIR method has since been rolled out to more states, so the Bihar verdict effectively became the template.

topics.title: No fundamental right to bet: the Supreme Court upholds the rummy and poker ban
topics.hook: The Supreme Court ruled on 27 May 2026 that Tamil Nadu and Karnataka can ban online rummy and poker played for money, holding that betting on a game of skill is still gambling, and gambling gets no protection under the right to trade.
topics.story:
Tamil Nadu and Karnataka had each tried, and each been blocked, before this. Tamil Nadu passed the Tamil Nadu Gaming and Police Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, then a further Online Gambling Act in 2022-23, widening the definition of gaming to catch rummy and poker played online for stakes. The Madras High Court struck the law down. Karnataka's equivalent law met the same fate at its own High Court. Both states argued that money changes the character of a game; both High Courts had held that rummy and poker are games of skill under settled law, and skill games enjoy a level of constitutional protection that pure games of chance do not.

The case, State of Tamil Nadu v. Junglee Games India Pvt. Ltd., reached the Supreme Court on appeal. A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan set aside both High Court rulings on 27 May 2026. The Court's reasoning turned the skill-versus-chance question, the one that had decided every previous round of this fight since the 1957 case that first drew the line for rummy, into a side issue. Once real money enters a game, the Court said, its constitutional character changes regardless of how much skill is involved: betting on a game of skill is still a gambling enterprise, and gambling is not a trade or business protected under Article 19(1)(g).

The Court accepted the states' argument that they were regulating a public health and public order problem, not restricting a trade. Both governments had presented data on gaming addiction, suicides linked to online betting losses, and the burden on family courts and police from gambling-related debt. The judgment effectively hands every state government the same tool: as long as a law targets games played for stakes rather than for free, it sits outside the fundamental right to trade and does not need to survive the reasonableness test Article 19(6) would otherwise demand.

The ruling lands at a moment when India's real-money gaming industry, built on fantasy sports, rummy and poker platforms, had grown into a business worth billions of dollars and drawn central-level attention too, with Parliament separately debating a law to regulate or restrict online money games at the national level. States now have Supreme Court cover to move first and move harder, and the ruling is likely to be cited well beyond gaming, in any future case about whether an activity built around stakes can claim the shelter of Article 19(1)(g) at all.

topics.title: India signs 10-year long-term agreement for Chabahar Port operation
topics.hook: India Global Ports Limited (IPGL) signed a 10-year contract with Iran's Ports and Maritime Organisation to equip and operate the Shahid Beheshti Terminal at Chabahar Port.
topics.story:
On 13 May 2026, Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal witnessed the signing of a landmark 10-year long-term bilateral contract in Tehran between India Ports Global Limited (IPGL) and Iran's Ports and Maritime Organization (PMO).

Under the agreement, IPGL will invest approximately $120 million in equipping the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar Port, alongside a $250 million credit window offered by India for infrastructure expansion. Chabahar, located in the Sistan-Baluchestan province on Iran's southeastern coast, provides India a bypass route to Afghanistan and Central Asia, avoiding Pakistan.

The port forms a key node in the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a 7,200-km multi-modal transit network linking India, Iran, Azerbaijan, and Russia. India's operational involvement in Chabahar counters China's presence at Pakistan's Gwadar port, located just 170 km east along the Gulf of Oman.

The United States State Department issued a caution regarding potential sanctions risks under the Iran Freedom and Counter-Proliferation Act (IFCA), though India maintains Chabahar's strategic exemption granted historically for humanitarian assistance to landlocked Afghanistan.

topics.title: The Supreme Court goes from 34 judges to 38
topics.hook: The Constitution never fixed the number. Parliament has raised it seven times, and the pendency argument has been the same each time.
topics.story:
The Union Cabinet cleared a proposal in May to raise the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court from **34 judges** to **38**, and the change requires an amendment to the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956**.

The number has never been in the Constitution. **Article 124(1)** provides for a Chief Justice and such number of other judges as Parliament may by law prescribe, and until Parliament does so the ceiling is seven. Parliament has raised it repeatedly: to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1978, 26 in 1986, 31 in 2009 and 34 in 2019. Every increase has been justified on the same ground, that the pendency of cases has outgrown the bench, and every increase has been followed within a few years by the same argument.

The pendency figures do carry the argument some distance. Around **83,000 cases** are pending in the Supreme Court, over **63 lakh** in the High Courts and more than **4.5 crore** in the district judiciary, and the district figure is the one that actually determines how long an ordinary litigant waits. Critics of the increase make two points. Adding judges to the apex court does nothing for the subordinate courts where the backlog sits, and a larger court sitting in more two-judge benches produces more conflicting decisions, which then need larger benches to resolve.

Appointments themselves still run through the **collegium**, the Chief Justice with the four next senior judges, which the Constitution does not mention and which the Court created for itself in the Second and Third Judges cases. The government's attempt to replace it with the **National Judicial Appointments Commission** was struck down in 2015. A higher sanctioned strength therefore enlarges the pool the collegium fills, and changes nothing about who fills it.

topics.title: Emergency medical care read into Article 21
topics.hook: A hospital that turns away a road accident victim for want of paperwork is now refusing a fundamental right, not just breaching an ethical rule.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court held in May that access to **emergency medical care** is part of the right to life under **Article 21**, and directed that no hospital, public or private, may refuse immediate treatment to a person in a medical emergency for want of documentation, police clearance or advance payment.

The holding sits on a line of cases rather than appearing from nowhere. **Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989)** had already held that every doctor, whether at a government hospital or in private practice, is obliged to extend medical aid to preserve life, and that no procedural formality may stand in the way. **Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal (1996)** went further and held the state liable in compensation where a man with head injuries was turned away by several government hospitals for want of beds, because Article 21 obliges the state to provide adequate medical facilities. The Court in 2026 pulled these together and made the obligation enforceable against private hospitals directly rather than through the state.

Article 21 has been the workhorse of Indian rights law for the same reason. **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** required any procedure depriving a person of life or liberty to be fair, just and reasonable, which converted the article from a procedural guarantee into a source of substantive rights. Courts have since read into it a right to livelihood, to a clean environment, to education for children until the Eighty-Sixth Amendment made it explicit in **Article 21A**, to privacy in **Puttaswamy (2017)**, and to die with dignity in **Common Cause (2018)**.

The practical question the judgment leaves open is enforcement. Refusal usually happens in the first minutes at a reception desk, where no court is watching, and the directions rely on state governments framing rules and on hospital licensing conditions carrying the obligation.

topics.title: Assam passes a Uniform Civil Code Bill
topics.hook: Article 44 tells the state to endeavour. It says nothing about which state.
topics.story:
The Assam Assembly passed a **Uniform Civil Code** Bill in May, following **Uttarakhand**, which enacted the first such state code in 2024 and brought it into force in January 2025. A state code covers marriage, divorce, succession, adoption and maintenance, and applies to residents of the state whether or not they live there.

The constitutional basis is **Article 44**, a Directive Principle which says the state shall endeavour to secure for citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India. Directive Principles are, by **Article 37**, not enforceable by any court, but fundamental in the governance of the country. The Constituent Assembly debated the article at length; **Ambedkar** argued that a uniform code was permissive and that no government would force it on an unwilling community, and members from the minority benches pressed unsuccessfully for an explicit consent requirement.

The state route works because personal law sits in **Entry 5 of the Concurrent List**, so both Parliament and a state legislature may legislate on marriage, divorce, adoption and succession. A state Bill touching on matters where a central law already exists needs the **President's assent under Article 254(2)** to prevail within the state. **Goa** is often described as already having a uniform code, though what it has is the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**, retained after 1961 and applying with several community-specific exceptions.

The legal arguments run in both directions. Supporters point to **Sarla Mudgal (1995)** and **Shah Bano (1985)**, where the Supreme Court urged the state to act on Article 44. Opponents argue that **Article 25**, freedom of religion, and the protection of tribal customary law are put at risk, which is why the Uttarakhand code exempted Scheduled Tribes and why the same question was raised in Assam, a state with substantial tribal populations under the **Sixth Schedule**.

topics.title: The RBI transfers ₹2.86 lakh crore to the Centre
topics.hook: A central bank does not have shareholders, so what it hands the government every August is not really a dividend, and the size of it is decided by a formula almost nobody reads.
topics.story:
The Reserve Bank's Central Board approved a surplus transfer of about **₹2.86 lakh crore** to the central government for the accounting year, a figure close to the record set the previous year and far above what the Budget had assumed.

The transfer is not a dividend in the corporate sense. Under **Section 47 of the RBI Act, 1934**, whatever remains of the Bank's profits after providing for bad debts, depreciation and staff funds is paid to the central government. The profits come mainly from interest on the Bank's holdings of government securities and foreign assets, from gains on the sale of foreign exchange, and increasingly from the difference between the exchange rate at which dollars were bought and the rate at which they are sold.

How much is retained rather than paid over is governed by an **economic capital framework** recommended by the **Bimal Jalan Committee** in 2019 and revised in 2025. The framework sets a **contingent risk buffer** as a band of the balance sheet size, and the revised version widened that band to **4.5% to 7.5%**. Anything above the chosen level flows to the government. A large transfer therefore reflects both a good year and a decision about how much cushion to keep.

For the Budget the money matters in a specific way. It appears under **non-tax revenue**, alongside dividends from public sector undertakings and spectrum receipts, and a transfer larger than budgeted gives the government room either to spend more or to hold the **fiscal deficit** below target without cutting anything. The recurring criticism is that a government which counts on this line is depending on an outcome it does not control, and that pressing a central bank for larger transfers erodes the independence the buffer is meant to protect.

topics.title: India takes the IORA chair and hosts the Indian Ocean Dialogue
topics.hook: Twenty-three countries around one ocean, and the only rule for joining is a coastline on it.
topics.story:
India assumed the chair of the **Indian Ocean Rim Association** for the **2025-27** term and hosted the tenth **Indian Ocean Dialogue** during the period. IORA was founded in **1997** at Mauritius as the Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation, renamed in 2013, and has its secretariat at **Ebene, Mauritius**. Membership is open to any sovereign state of the Indian Ocean rim; it now has **23 members** and eleven dialogue partners, including China, the United States, Japan and the European Union. **Pakistan** has applied and been blocked, as consensus is required.

The grouping works through six priority areas: maritime safety and security, trade and investment facilitation, fisheries management, disaster risk management, academic and science cooperation, and tourism, with the blue economy and women's economic empowerment added as cross-cutting themes. It has no security function and no standing force, which is both its limitation and the reason a membership this diverse holds together.

India's own framing has moved on. The **SAGAR** doctrine, Security and Growth for All in the Region, announced at Mauritius in 2015, was recast in 2025 as **MAHASAGAR**, Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions, extending the same idea to Africa and the wider Global South. Alongside it India runs the **Information Fusion Centre for the Indian Ocean Region** at Gurugram, which shares merchant shipping data with partner navies, and the **Colombo Security Conclave** with Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Mauritius and Bangladesh.

The context is competition. Chinese port investment and naval deployment across the ocean, the reopening of the Red Sea route after Houthi attacks disrupted it, and the **India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor** agreed at the 2023 G20 all run through the same water.

facts.v: 1997 at Mauritius; renamed IORA in 2013; secretariat at Ebene

2025-27 term; hosted the tenth Indian Ocean Dialogue

topics.title: The EU carbon border tax goes live and India objects
topics.hook: A tariff that calls itself a climate measure, on goods that were never made in Europe.
topics.story:
The European Union's **Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism** entered its definitive phase from **1 January 2026**, after a transitional period from October 2023 in which importers only had to report. From now importers must buy **CBAM certificates** priced against the EU Emissions Trading System to cover the embedded emissions of covered goods, with a deduction for any carbon price already paid in the country of origin.

The covered sectors are **iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen**, chosen because they are emissions-intensive and exposed to trade. For India the first two matter most: steel and aluminium make up a large share of what India sells into the EU, and the EU is one of India's largest export markets.

India's objection has three parts. The mechanism is a unilateral trade measure dressed as climate policy, and so sits awkwardly with the **common but differentiated responsibilities** principle written into the UNFCCC and repeated in the Paris Agreement. It discriminates in effect against developing producers whose grids are coal-heavy, since the emissions are measured at the point of production. And it may violate **GATT** rules on national treatment and most favoured nation, an argument India has raised at the WTO Committee on Trade and Environment while stopping short of a formal dispute. India has also said it would consider a **retaliatory levy** if the measure is applied without accommodation, and has pushed the issue into the India-EU free trade negotiations.

The domestic response is a **carbon credit trading scheme** notified under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022, with a compliance mechanism for energy-intensive industries. If Indian producers pay a domestic carbon price, that price is deductible against the CBAM certificate cost, which turns a transfer to Brussels into revenue collected at home.

topics.title: India and Vietnam move to the top tier of partnership
topics.hook: India has about thirty strategic partnerships. Only a handful sit at the top of the ladder, and the rungs mean something.
topics.story:
India and Vietnam upgraded their relationship to an **Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership** in May, with a trade target of about **$25 billion by 2030** and expanded defence and maritime cooperation.

The ladder of Indian partnership labels runs roughly from a plain strategic partnership, through a comprehensive strategic partnership, to the special or enhanced versions reserved for a few. Vietnam had been a **Comprehensive Strategic Partner** since **2016**, one of the first countries in Southeast Asia to reach that level, and the two had already signed a **Joint Vision for Peace, Prosperity and People** in 2020.

Defence is the substance. India extended a **$500 million** defence line of credit, has delivered patrol vessels built at Larsen and Toubro's Kattupalli yard, trains Vietnamese submariners and fighter pilots, and gifted a decommissioned corvette. The **BrahMos** missile has been discussed for years and has been sold to the Philippines, which makes Vietnam the obvious next customer. India's **ONGC Videsh** holds exploration blocks in Vietnamese waters that China's nine-dash line claim overlaps, which is where the two countries' positions on the **South China Sea** converge: both insist on the **UN Convention on the Law of the Sea** and on the 2016 arbitral award that rejected the nine-dash line.

The relationship sits inside **Act East**, which the Look East policy of 1992 became in 2014, and inside the **India-ASEAN** framework where Vietnam has often carried India's case. Vietnam is one of the four ASEAN claimants in the South China Sea, along with the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei, and its balancing act between Washington and Beijing has made it a useful partner for a country doing something similar.

topics.title: India-UAE trade crosses $100 billion
topics.hook: A trade agreement negotiated in eighty-eight days, and the target it set for 2030 was met four years early.
topics.story:
Bilateral trade between India and the United Arab Emirates crossed **$100 billion**, the target the two countries had set for 2030 when they signed their **Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement**. The agreement was negotiated in about **eighty-eight days**, signed in **February 2022** and in force from **1 May 2022**, and it was India's first trade deal of its kind in a decade.

The CEPA removed tariffs on the large majority of tariff lines, phased over several years, and covers services, government procurement, digital trade and intellectual property. Indian gems and jewellery, textiles, engineering goods and pharmaceuticals gained; the UAE's petroleum products and its role as a re-export hub gained on the other side. The UAE is India's third largest trading partner after the United States and China, and its second largest export destination.

Beyond trade the relationship has three legs. **Energy**: the UAE is a major crude supplier and holds capacity in India's **strategic petroleum reserve** at Mangaluru and Padur, with further agreements on LNG storage. **Payments**: the two central banks agreed in 2023 to settle bilateral trade in rupees and dirhams and to link the **UPI** with the UAE's instant payment platform, which cuts the cost of remittances sent by a diaspora of roughly **3.5 million** Indians, the largest expatriate group in the country. **Connectivity**: the UAE is a signatory to the **India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor** agreed at the G20 in New Delhi in 2023, and the corridor's eastern leg runs from Indian ports to Jebel Ali.

The newer additions are in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centres, where Emirati sovereign funds have committed capital to Indian projects and Indian firms have taken space in Emirati compute capacity.
